title: Start fog or smoke gave no clear survey-duration contrast in four Canada and US samples in 1985-2024
abstract: We tested whether bird surveys that started in fog or smoke took longer than those that started in clear sky. We used 64,867 accepted North American Breeding Bird Survey runs from Canada and the US in two periods, 1985-2004 and 2005-2024. Four separate models controlled route-observer effects, state-year effects, start weather, date and start time. Adjusted contrasts were +0.37, +1.67, +1.13 and +0.48 minutes. All four intervals included zero after correction for four tests. An added end-weather control gave a positive interval only in the early US sample. Thus the primary test did not establish a repeated delay. The sky code combines fog and smoke. Selected survey conditions, rare reports, coarse timing and unmeasured road conditions limit inference. Elapsed time includes travel and recording. This test does not measure pollution damage, true richness, climate-change effects or time spent counting. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes and external retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: Start fog-or-smoke contrasts in elapsed survey minutes. Bars are approximate intervals corrected for four primary tests. All cross zero.

citations.reason: We adapt parsing and regression code for a new elapsed-time outcome and start-weather design. The source records overlap.
Prior duration study used start temperature. We test the fog-or-smoke start code with a later source release.
